title: Can you find all the different nets of a cube?
description: The nets of a cube are sorted by their longest row of squares, and each family is counted once turns and flips are removed. The board adds the families and checks that the total is the number the question gives.
teaching_notes: One idea: sort the nets by the longest row of squares so that none is counted twice or missed. Watch for students who count a turned or flipped net as a new one.

video_script.why: The child finds every net of a cube by sorting the nets into families, because nets that turn or flip into each other are the same net.
video_script.substitution: families by the longest row: four (6 nets), three (3 nets with a row of three in the middle and 1 net of two rows of three), two (the staircase, 1 net); total 11.
video_script.anchor: the nets of a cube drawn family by family on the stage
video_script.payoff_line: Six nets have a row of four, four have a row of three, and one is a staircase

final_answer.value: 6 nets with a row of four, 4 with a longest row of three, and 1 staircase: 11 in all
final_answer.spoken: six nets with a row of four, four with a longest row of three, and one staircase, eleven in all

hold_back: 6 nets with a row of four, 4 with a longest row of three, and 1 staircase
maths_rules: row of four with one square above and one below: 4 x 4 = 16 placings, 6 different nets after turns and flips (Burnside: (16 + 4 + 4 + 0) / 4 = 6)
longest row of three with one square on one side and two on the other: 3 nets
two rows of three joined at one square: 1 net
family counts: 6 with a row of four, 3 + 1 = 4 with a longest row of three, 1 staircase
video_script.design: One idea: sort by the longest row. Each family appears as small nets on the stage, and a counter adds up the families at the end.
